title: Jizyah and the Spread of Islam
lede: A short book by a philosopher and Islamicist on jizya, the poll tax Islamic states levied on non-Muslims who kept their faith. Narain first sets out its theory: since “the earth belongs to Allah”, unbelievers live on as tributaries, the dhimmis. He traces its origins to a pre-Islamic Persian head tax. Then he follows it through India's history and argues that it did much to spread Islam, because paying stopped the day one converted.
facts: dirhams a year: the three classes of jizya from Muhammad bin Qasim to Aurangzeb
first levied in India, in Sindh, with Brahmins and ascetics exempt
Aurangzeb reimposes it after Akbar had abolished it
Kashmir's jizya finally lifted, when Akbar annexed the valley
note: Narain argues as a critic. Historians agree that jizya was levied unevenly and was often hard to collect, as he himself notes. They differ on how much it drove conversion. This page follows his account and attributes his judgements to him.

sections.title: When and where it was levied
sections.lede: Narain's dates for jizya in force (orange) and lifted (blue), with Kashmir shown separately. In between, he says, it stayed “in force with varying degrees of emphasis but with brief intervals”.
items: Muhammad bin Qasim: 48, 24 or 12 dirhams a head. Brahmins and ascetics exempt.
Iltutmish's ulema urge “Islam or death”. Alauddin's qazi preaches humiliation.
Firoz Tughlaq extends it to Brahmins
Brahmins threaten self-immolation. Other castes pay on their behalf.
Imposed for the first time, along with zakat on Hindus
Reimposed on Brahmins at their thread ceremony
Yusuf Shah suspends it, and it ends with Mughal annexation
Kept off by Jahangir and Shah Jahan, though Bijapur went on collecting
Old rates, with the old rituals of humiliation
sections.note: Dates are from the book, except the year of Akbar's abolition (1564), which Narain does not give and is added from the standard histories. Colour: orange for levied, blue for not levied.

sections.title: Three classes of taxpayer
sections.lede: The same three tiers appear in Muhammad bin Qasim's Sindh and in Aurangzeb's 1679 order. Under Aurangzeb, the top class meant an income of 10,000 dirhams or more a year, and the middle class over 200.
items: “24 silver rupees” a head under Qasim
Qasim levied 12 dirhams on merchants and artisans “as they had already lost their property by plunder”

sections.title: The logic Narain reconstructs
items: Through Allah and the Prophet, land belongs to the Muslim community.
Hanafi law alone lets polytheists live on by paying.
Protected but subordinate, with set humiliations when paying.
Payment stops at once. Firoz Tughlaq boasts that Hindus came “in clusters after clusters”.

sections.title: How it was resisted
items: Hindus gathered in their hundreds of thousands to petition Aurangzeb. Narain says elephants were driven into the crowd.
Variously attributed to Shivaji, Sambhaji, Jaswant Singh and Rana Raj Singh. It mocks an emperor “envying the bowls of beggars”.
Local chiefs often refused, and even Aurangzeb complained it was hard to collect.
Jonaraja calls it the durdanda, the “ignoble penalty”, and the turushka-danda, the Turks' tax.

sections.q: Did the dhimmis not enjoy the concession of the Shari'ah, all trace of the Hindus would vanish.
sections.cite: Amir Khusrau, quoted by Narain as evidence that jizya was the Hindus' price of survival
